steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper on estimating neighborhood-level socioeconomic indicators (population density, income, education) for U.S. census block groups from high-resolution aerial imagery with machine learning. It should motivate the problem, state our objective and contributions, and outline the rest of the paper.

- Traditional data sources vs. remote sensing and machine learning; technical challenges
- Our objective: three metrics at the block group level
- Study setup: cities and the two methodologies
- Contributions
- Paper structure

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Why measurement matters
  - censuses/surveys expensive, time-consuming
  - long gaps between surveys in developing countries -> hinders public policy
  - needed for: progress toward targets (UN Sustainable Development Goals), accountability, evidence-based decisions, interventions for well-being
  - identify areas/populations needing most attention and resources
  - quantify urbanization, education levels, healthcare access, income -> find vulnerable groups, targeted interventions, resource allocation
- Data sources and remote sensing
  - traditional: national accounts, household surveys, administrative records (tax filings)
  - expensive even where collected
  - neighborhood conditions change drastically in short periods
  - -> need faster, cheaper estimation between neighborhoods
  - since 1990s: nighttime light intensity (satellite/aircraft sensors), large-scale approximations
  - from ~2016: ML (esp. neural networks) on high-res daytime imagery, finer scale
  - aerial imagery + ML effective for monitoring environment, tracking socioeconomic stats
  - challenges: images cover vast areas, too large for CV networks at high res; irregular neighborhood shapes; survey stats aggregated at different levels
- Objective
  - ML on high-res aerial imagery, U.S. Census block group (~neighborhood)
  - population density; Median Household Income (MHI); educational attainment (% with at least bachelor's)
  - feasibility study: where and how people live between neighborhoods
  - relevant UN goals 1 (poverty reduction), 4 (well-being improvement), 10 (within-country inequality reduction)
- Setup
  - 94 of the 100 largest U.S. cities by GDP
  - spatial features (roads, parks, buildings) related to census variables
  - supervised CNN; semi-supervised bag-of-visual-words (BoVW), interpretable representations
- Contributions
  - aerial imagery resolves socioeconomic features at neighborhood scale
  - supervised / semi-supervised clustering explain 81% / 61% of variation in population density
- Structure: II literature, III data, IV methods, V results, VI limitations, VII conclusion

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Collecting socioeconomic data with censuses and other surveys costs a lot and takes a long time. Because of this there is often a long gap between surveys in developing countries, and that makes it hard to formulate appropriate public policies. Being able to measure socioeconomic metrics is essential for many things: evaluating progress toward targets (for example the United Nations' Sustainable Development Goals), promoting accountability, enabling evidence-based decision-making, and giving a basis for informed actions and interventions that improve human well-being. Measurements help find the areas and populations that need the most attention and resources. When development indicators like urbanization, education levels, healthcare access, and income are quantified, policymakers and development practitioners can identify the most vulnerable and disadvantaged groups and design targeted interventions for their specific needs and optimize resource allocation.

Traditionally these metrics are measured with national accounts data, household surveys, and administrative records like tax filings. Even where this data is collected, it is expensive. Also, at the neighborhood level socioeconomic conditions can change drastically in very short periods of time. So it is important to explore faster and cheaper techniques for estimating important socioeconomic outcomes between neighborhoods. Since the 1990s, nighttime light intensity from remote sensing technologies, such as sensors on satellites and aircraft, has been analyzed and has helped approximate development and socioeconomic metrics at large scales. Starting around 2016, analyzing remotely sensed data (often high-resolution daytime imagery) with machine learning methods, especially neural networks, became popular very quickly and made finer scale approximations possible. These techniques have shown in general that analyzing aerial imagery with machine learning is an effective way to remotely monitor the natural and built environment and to estimate and track development and socioeconomic statistics. There are technical challenges in this research, because aerial images can cover vast areas and at higher resolutions they can be too large to put directly into computer vision networks. The often irregular shapes of neighborhoods make it more complex, and so does the fact that survey statistics are aggregated at different levels across different geographical areas.

Our objective. In this paper we look at whether machine learning models trained on high-resolution aerial imagery can estimate the following metrics at the U.S. Census block group level (which is about the size of a neighborhood):

- Population density
- Median Household Income (MHI)
- Educational attainment (% of the population with at least a bachelor's degree)

This paper is a feasibility study of how well aerial photography and machine learning can detect where and how people live between neighborhoods. The UN sustainable development goals that could benefit specifically from measuring neighborhood density, income, and education conditions include goals 1 (poverty reduction), 4 (well-being improvement), and 10 (within-country inequality reduction).

- Setup
  - 94 of the 100 largest U.S. cities by GDP
  - features like roads, parks, buildings quantified and related to census variables
  - two methods: supervised CNN, semi-supervised BoVW (simplified, interpretable representations of census blocks)
- Contributions
  - contemporary aerial imagery resolves socioeconomic features at neighborhood scale
  - supervised learning 81%, semi-supervised clustering 61% of variation in population density
- Paper structure: Sections II-VII (literature, data, methods, results, limitations, conclusion)

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Collecting socioeconomic data with censuses and other surveys costs a lot and takes a long time. Because of this there is often a long gap between surveys in developing countries, and that makes it hard to formulate appropriate public policies. Being able to measure socioeconomic metrics is essential for many things: evaluating progress toward targets (for example the United Nations' Sustainable Development Goals), promoting accountability, enabling evidence-based decision-making, and giving a basis for informed actions and interventions that improve human well-being. Measurements help find the areas and populations that need the most attention and resources. When development indicators like urbanization, education levels, healthcare access, and income are quantified, policymakers and development practitioners can identify the most vulnerable and disadvantaged groups and design targeted interventions for their specific needs and optimize resource allocation.

Traditionally these metrics are measured with national accounts data, household surveys, and administrative records like tax filings. Even where this data is collected, it is expensive. Also, at the neighborhood level socioeconomic conditions can change drastically in very short periods of time. So it is important to explore faster and cheaper techniques for estimating important socioeconomic outcomes between neighborhoods. Since the 1990s, nighttime light intensity from remote sensing technologies, such as sensors on satellites and aircraft, has been analyzed and has helped approximate development and socioeconomic metrics at large scales. Starting around 2016, analyzing remotely sensed data (often high-resolution daytime imagery) with machine learning methods, especially neural networks, became popular very quickly and made finer scale approximations possible. These techniques have shown in general that analyzing aerial imagery with machine learning is an effective way to remotely monitor the natural and built environment and to estimate and track development and socioeconomic statistics. There are technical challenges in this research, because aerial images can cover vast areas and at higher resolutions they can be too large to put directly into computer vision networks. The often irregular shapes of neighborhoods make it more complex, and so does the fact that survey statistics are aggregated at different levels across different geographical areas.

Our objective. In this paper we look at whether machine learning models trained on high-resolution aerial imagery can estimate the following metrics at the U.S. Census block group level (which is about the size of a neighborhood):

- Population density
- Median Household Income (MHI)
- Educational attainment (% of the population with at least a bachelor's degree)

This paper is a feasibility study of how well aerial photography and machine learning can detect where and how people live between neighborhoods. The UN sustainable development goals that could benefit specifically from measuring neighborhood density, income, and education conditions include goals 1 (poverty reduction), 4 (well-being improvement), and 10 (within-country inequality reduction).

We train and test models on 94 of the 100 largest U.S. cities by gross domestic product (GDP). Spatial features in urban settings are extracted automatically, so variations in city infrastructure like roads, parks, and buildings can be quantified and related to the census variables. We use two methodologies. One is driven by a supervised convolutional neural network (CNN). The other is a semi-supervised framework that uses bag-of-visual-words (BoVW) to make simplified but interpretable representations of census blocks.

The main contributions of this paper are:

1. We demonstrate that contemporary aerial imagery can resolve features related to socioeconomic variables at the scale of a neighborhood;
2. We find that supervised learning and semi-supervised clustering of image patches can explain 81% and 61% of the variation in neighborhood population density, respectively.

Paper structure. The rest of the paper is organized like this. Section II gives an overview of existing literature on estimating poverty, population, and other socioeconomic indicators from aerial imagery with machine learning. Section III explains how the image and annotation data are acquired, fused, and processed. Section IV describes our methods, including the supervised and semi-supervised learning approaches. Section V presents the results, and Section VI analyzes and discusses the limitations of our work. Section VII gives concluding remarks.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Censuses and other surveys administered to collect socioeconomic data are expensive and time-consuming [1]. For this reason, there is often a long gap between surveys in developing countries, which hinders the appropriate formulation of public policies. The ability to measure socioeconomic metrics is essential for evaluating progress toward targets (such as the United Nations' Sustainable Development Goals [2]), promoting accountability, enabling evidence-based decision-making, and providing a basis for informed actions and interventions to improve human well-being [3,4]. Measurements help determine the areas and populations that require the most attention and resources [5]. By quantifying development indicators such as urbanization, education levels, healthcare access, and income, policymakers and development practitioners can identify the most vulnerable and disadvantaged groups, design targeted interventions for their specific needs, and optimize resource allocation [6,5,7].

Such metrics are traditionally measured through national accounts data, household surveys, and administrative records such as tax filings [1]. Even in regions where such data are collected, they are expensive [8]. Furthermore, socioeconomic conditions at the neighborhood level can change drastically in very short periods of time [9]. It is therefore imperative to explore faster and more cost-effective techniques for estimating vital socioeconomic outcomes between neighborhoods. Since the 1990s, analysis of nighttime light intensity from remote sensing technologies, such as sensors onboard satellites and aircraft, has effectively contributed to approximating development and socioeconomic metrics at large scales [10,11]. Beginning around 2016, analysis of remotely sensed data (often high-resolution daytime imagery) with machine learning methods, particularly neural networks, has rapidly grown in popularity and enabled finer scale approximations. These techniques have broadly shown that analyzing aerial imagery with machine learning is an effective strategy to remotely monitor the natural and built environment and to estimate and track development and socioeconomic statistics [12]. Technical challenges arise in this line of research because aerial images can cover vast areas and, at higher resolutions, be too large to input directly into computer vision networks. This is further complicated by the often irregular shapes of neighborhoods and the aggregation of survey statistics at different levels across various geographical areas.

Our objective. In this paper, we investigate the potential of machine learning models trained on high-resolution aerial imagery to estimate the following metrics at the U.S. Census block group level (approximately the size of a neighborhood):

- Population density
- Median Household Income (MHI)
- Educational attainment (% of the population with at least a bachelor's degree)

This paper is a feasibility study of how well aerial photography and machine learning can detect where and how people live between neighborhoods. UN sustainable development goals that may benefit specifically from measuring neighborhood density, income, and education conditions include goals 1 (poverty reduction), 4 (well-being improvement), and 10 (within-country inequality reduction) [2].

We carry out our investigation by training and testing models on 94 of the 100 largest U.S. cities by gross domestic product (GDP). By automatically extracting spatial features in urban settings, variations in city infrastructure, such as roads, parks, and buildings, can be quantified and related to the census variables. Two methodologies are employed: one driven by a supervised convolutional neural network (CNN), and the other by a semi-supervised framework that uses bag-of-visual-words (BoVW) to generate simplified but interpretable representations of census blocks.

The most notable contributions of this paper are:

1. Demonstration that contemporary aerial imagery can resolve features related to socioeconomic variables at the scale of a neighborhood;
2. Finding that supervised learning and semi-supervised clustering of image patches can respectively explain 81% and 61% of the variation in neighborhood population density.

Paper structure. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II gives an overview of the existing literature on estimating poverty, population, and other socioeconomic indicators from aerial imagery with machine learning. Section III details how the image and annotation data are acquired, fused, and processed. Section IV describes our methods, including the supervised and semi-supervised learning approaches. We then present results in Section V and analyze and discuss the limitations of our work in Section VI. Concluding remarks are offered in Section VII.

[2] United Nations Department of Economic and Social Affairs. The 17 goals of sustainable development. https://sdgs.un.org/goals .
